questions.stem: The student wants to explain the limits of invariants to an audience unfamiliar with knot theory. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A knot invariant assigns a value to a knot diagram.
  • Deforming the diagram without cutting leaves the value unchanged.
  • Two diagrams with different values must be different knots.
  • Two diagrams with the same value may still be different knots.
  • No invariant known distinguishes every pair of distinct knots.

choices.label: A
choices.content: A knot invariant assigns a value to a diagram, and deforming the diagram leaves that value unchanged.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Two diagrams with different values must be different knots, and deformation never changes a value.

choices.label: C
choices.content: No invariant known distinguishes every pair of distinct knots, though each assigns a value to a diagram.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Differing values prove that two diagrams are different knots, but matching values prove nothing, and no known invariant separates every pair.

questions.stem: The student wants to emphasise that the stronger join is not always the one a rigger wants. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A knot costs a rope about a third of its strength where it bends round itself.
  • A splice tucks the strands of one rope in among another's.
  • A spliced join keeps most of the rope's strength.
  • A splice takes far longer to make than a knot.
  • A splice cannot be cast off in a hurry.

choices.label: A
choices.content: A splice keeps most of a rope's strength where a knot costs about a third of it, but a splice cannot be cast off in a hurry, so a join that may have to be let go quickly is knotted instead.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A knot costs a rope about a third of its strength where it bends round itself, and a splice takes far longer to make.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A splice tucks the strands of one rope in among another's and keeps most of the rope's strength.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A splice takes far longer to make than a knot does and cannot be cast off in a hurry.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.content: Roots cannot enter the fine soil pores from which the fungus draws phosphorus.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Seedlings cut off from the fungal network grew more slowly than seedlings left connected to it.

A rope fails in a cascade, and the total it can bear is always less than the sum of its parts.

choices.label: A

questions.stem: According to the text, what does the tree gain from the fungus?

questions.passage: The fungal threads that sheathe a tree's roots take sugar from the tree and pass back phosphorus drawn from a volume of soil the roots could never reach. choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.content: A supply of sugar that supplements what its leaves produce.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A faster rate of growth in the absence of light.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Access to phosphorus from soil beyond the reach of its own roots.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Elstad's argument?

questions.passage: A bacterial population exposed to an antibiotic can recover its numbers within days, and it is usually assumed that the survivors carry a resistance gene. Microbiologist Tomas Elstad argues that in some populations the survivors are not genetically different at all, but simply happen to be dormant when the drug arrives.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Resistance genes were detected in a small fraction of the cells before treatment began.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Higher doses of the antibiotic killed a larger fraction of the population.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Survivors regrown from a treated culture were no more resistant to a second dose than the original population had been, and their descendants died at the usual rate.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The treated cultures took several days longer to recover than untreated cultures took to reach the same density.

questions.passage: Mycorrhizal fungi are often described as passing carbon between trees, but carbon moving out of one tree and into a fungus need not reach a second tree at all. Ecologist Solveig Naess argues that most of what leaves a mature tree by this route is consumed by the fungus itself.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The quantity of carbon leaving a mature tree rose when the tree was shaded.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Labelled carbon fed to a mature tree was recovered in large quantities in fungal tissue and in only trace amounts in the neighbouring seedlings connected to the same network.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Seedlings connected to a network grew faster than seedlings isolated from it.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Fungal networks were found to link trees of several different species in the same stand.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Liest's argument?

choices.label: D
choices.content: The charcoal from the hearths was well enough preserved to give a precise date.

  • Fibre from stalks lifted too early will not part from the core.
  • Fibre from stalks left in too long crumbles when it is combed.
  • The soaking is stopped when the fibre feels ready, not after a set number of days.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The soaking is stopped when the fibre feels ready rather than after a set number of days.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Fibre from stalks that were left in the water too long crumbles when it is combed.

4x + 3y = k
x - y = 2
